newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands brace for evacuation in east Germany.
newsitem.headline: Thousands brace for evacuation in east Germany.

text.p: Thousands of people in east Germany braced for evacuation on Sunday, as the Oder River on the Polish border rose and more dike breaches were reported.
Local officials warned 19,000 people to be prepared to leave their homes at a moment's notice. Around 5,000 were evacuated from the Oderbruch plains area on Friday.

"We are preparing the entire Oderbruch region for a possible evacuation," said Ralph Leidenheimer, a spokesman for the Brandenburg interior ministry. "There is an acute danger that the dike could break."

Officials said water levels north of the town of Brieskow-Finkenheerd, where a dike section one km (half a mile) long was swept away overnight, were rising as flood water trapped inland flowed back into the river.
The water levels around Frankfurt an der Oder, the largest German city in the region, had risen half a metre since the night before by early afternoon on Sunday, the officials said.

Some of the worst floods this century throughout central Europe have claimed over 100 lives in Poland and the Czech Republic this month. Germany has escaped the worst of the floods, but damage to homes and crops has been extensive.
Seven years after 1990 unification, officials say flood damage could destroy many east Germans financially, particularly farmers, just starting to get on their feet.

The worst damage would hit the Oderbruch plateau north of Frankfurt an der Oder -- a vast plain some 50 km (30 miles) long and 17 km (11 miles) km wide that was created 250 years ago by Frederick the Great, who drained the moors and redirected the flow of the river Oder to create the fertile basin for farmland.

But because the area is considerably lower than the river itself, any serious break in the 70-km section of dike protecting the Oderbruch would flood the entire region in a matter of hours, submerging some 17 villages and ruining crops.

Large sections of the dike in Oderbruch have collapsed over the past few days, but thousands of German soldiers, aid workers and local residents have worked round-the-clock shifts for days to prevent a break.

Soldiers criss-crossed the Oderbruch plains with a system of secondary dikes, a second line of defence in the event of a break in the main dike, which was built between 1747 and 1753 by the Dutch engineer Simon Leonhard van Haerlem.

Further south, the floods ripped out a one-km section of dike early on Sunday in Brieskow-Finkenheerd, flooding villages and forcing 67 people to flee their homes. Emergency teams of up to 12,000 soldiers, border guards and volunteers were working constantly to shore up other parts of the dike.
Neighbouring villages Wiesenau and Ziltendorf have been under water for the past two days after the dike broke there.

Streets in the two villages were submerged and only the tops of houses and trees were visible. Local villagers stood in shorts and sandals next to sand bag barricades erected in their streets to block the steadily creeping tide of water.
